# How AI literacy correlates with affective, behavioral, cognitive and contextual variables: A systematic review

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

### Arne Bewersdorff [a,\*](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence) [,](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9725-268X) Claudia Nerdel [a,](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence) Xiaoming Zhai [b](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence)

a _Technical University of Munich, Germany_ b _University of Georgia, USA_

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ This systematic review maps the empirical landscape of AI literacy by examining its correlations with a diverse 

AI literacy array of affective, behavioral, cognitive and contextual variables. Building on the review of AI literacy scales by Systematic review Lintner (2024), we analyzed 31 empirical studies that applied six of those AI literacy scales, covering 14 Cognitive and affective factors

countries and a range of participant groups. Our findings reveal robust correlations of AI literacy with AI self- 

Education Measurement efficacy, positive AI attitudes, motivation, and digital competencies, and negative correlations with AI anxiety 

and negative AI attitudes. Personal factors such as age appear largely uncorrelated with AI literacy. The review reveals measurement challenges regarding AI literacy: discrepancies between self-assessment scales and performance-based tests suggest that metacognitive biases like the Dunning Kruger effect may inflate certain correlations with self-assessment AI literacy scales. Despite these challenges, the robust findings provide a solid 

foundation for future research.

Based on the above objectives, this study aims to answer five research questions: 

RQ1: What is the scope and nature of the empirical evidence on correlations between AI literacy and other variables?

RQ2: Which robust correlations between AI literacy and other vari- ables were consistently identified across various AI literacy in- struments and target populations?

RQ3: What inconsistent findings emerged from the reported studies on AI literacy correlations?

RQ4: How are different scales (self-assessment vs. performance- based) associated with the observed correlations?

RQ5: What research gaps exist in the literature regarding the employed instruments, investigated variables, and samples?

## 2. Theoretical background

### _2.1._ _AI literacy_

Although numerous frameworks for conceptualizing AI literacy have emerged in recent years, they converge on a broadly shared under- standing of the construct (overview: [Laupichler et al., 2022)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). A common thread is the recognition of its multifaceted nature, which integrates not only technical knowledge but also ethical implications and practical competencies. As one example, the prominent framework by [Long and Magerko (2020)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) defines AI literacy as “a set of competencies that en- ables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace”. They define 17 competencies (e.g., “Human Role in AI”) based on five guiding questions (What is AI? What can AI do? How does AI work? How should AI be used? and How do people perceive AI?).

### _2.2._ _Measurement of AI literacy_

While many AI literacy scales are self-assessment scales, some AI literacy scales are performance-based assessments (for comparison see [Lintner, 2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). These two different types of scales have inherent prop- erties that might yield two distinct outcomes regarding the measured variable. While performance-based scales aim to objectively measure actual knowledge open to intersubjective verification, self-assessment scales measure the individual’s perception of their knowledge. Self-assessment scales are straightforward to administer across large populations. Given the challenges of developing and updating extensive objective test instruments in a fast-changing field like AI, self-assessment scales provide a flexible and scalable option. On the other hand, self- assessment scales are subject to metacognitive biases such as the Dun- ning–Kruger effect ([Dunning & Kruger, 1999)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational), in which low performers may overestimate and high performers may underestimate their abili- ties. They are also vulnerable to the self-enhancement bias ([Brown, 1986)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational), a broader tendency for individuals to view themselves more favorably than justified. This subjectivity might result in lower construct validity and can make it difficult to uncover the ways AI literacy actually interacts with other variables.

Performance-based assessments can minimize such bias through their objectivity, but come with their own challenges, such as test-taking strategies and guessing ([Crocker & Algina, 1986)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). While both types of assessment scales claim to assess AI literacy, until now it remains un- clear if they actually capture the same construct and if they correlate in comparable strength with surrounding variables.

### _2.3._ _The ABC-framework_

The ABC-framework ([Fredricks et al., 2004)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) conceptualizes 

engagement as the interplay of affective (emotions and attitudes), behavioral (observable actions and habits) and cognitive (knowledge and mental processes) components. Rather than operating as isolated dimensions, affect, behavior, and cognition are interrelated within the individual. The affective dimension captures internal states such as at- titudes and emotions like anxiety. The behavioral dimension focuses on planned and observable actions and habits. The cognitive dimension addresses mental processes and knowledge, including critical thinking and problem-solving.

This flexible affect- behavior- and cognition-framework (ABC- framework) is particularly valuable for investigating complex, multi- faceted phenomena across various contexts as it provides a flexible, yet theory-informed, structure that can accommodate diverse constructs. The ABC framework will serve to structure the findings of this review.

### _2.4._ _Correlations between AI literacy and affective, behavioral, cognitive, and surrounding variables_

Regarding the correlations between affective, behavioral, cognitive, and surrounding variables, there are well-established findings from other fields beyond AI. Studies show strong correlations between knowledge (cognition) and attitudes ([Allum et al., 2008;](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) [Bybee & McCrae, 2011)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). According to [Bandura’s Social Cognitive Theory (2003),](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) there is a strong connection between a person’s literacy skills and their self-efficacy. This relationship with self-efficacy was shown by [Carmi-](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) [chael et al. (2010)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) in the context of mathematical achievement. Simi- larly, [Getenet et al. (2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) and Prior et al. (2016) demonstrate that digital literacy plays a pivotal role in enhancing students’ digital self-efficacy, thereby reinforcing the empirical connection between lit- eracy and self-efficacy across multiple domains.

Assumptions about the connection between technology use (behavior) and technological literacy (cognition) often draw on the ‘digital native’ idea, presuming that frequent users possess sophisticated digital knowledge. Yet, in reality, frequent users are often limited to basic skills ([Kirschner & De Bruyckere, 2017)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). The nature of AI use itself may be a key factor influencing thecorrelation between AI use and AI literacy, as [Koch et al. (2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) suggested based on their findings that individuals who use AI may become more AI literate. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM; [Davis, 1989)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) suggests that higher literacy levels enable users to overcome barriers to adoption and influence their attitudes and behavioral intentions toward its use. The Theory of Plan- ned Behavior ([Ajzen, 1991)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) and the TAM both suggest that a person’s knowledge significantly influences their behavioral intentions. This theoretical perspective supports the expectation that higher AI literacy should be correlated with more positive AI attitudes, greater AI self-efficacy, and increased AI usage.

Surrounding variables, including socio-economic background, insti- tutional support, and access to digital resources, are crucial contextual factors that may influence the development of AI literacy. Regarding surrounding variables, Bourdieu’s theory of cultural capital posits that an individual’s socioeconomic background and access to resources are crucial for literacy development ([Bourdieu, 1986;](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) empirical evidence see e.g. [Kang & Cogan, 2022)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). However, its applicability to AI literacy is ambiguous. Unlike traditional literacy, AI literacy could be developed through free online courses and accessible digital resources, potentially reducing the reliance on cultural capital. Moreover, AI technology itself may enhance access to educational resources, challenging conventional assumptions about the necessity of pre-existing cultural capital for acquiring literacy. Overall, correlations between AI literacy and back- ground and surrounding variables remain largely elusive. Given these conceptual and measurement challenges, a systematic review is necessary to clarify the correlations between AI literacy and related affective, behavioral, cognitive, and contextual variables. Such a review will help identify not only robust correlations but also areas where further empirical work is needed. Pinpointing these relationships offers concrete benefits: it shows curriculum designers which 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.**

dispositions (e.g., AI anxiety, AI attitudes) are most strongly linked to AI literacy, alerts instrument developers to when self-assessment is suffi- cient and when performance tests are indispensable, and signals policy- makers where additional institutional support might be required to narrow literacy disparities. In this way, the review provides an evidence- based roadmap for targeted educational interventions, more precise assessment strategies, and future causal studies that can build on the most promising correlates.

## 3. Method

### _3.1._ _Search procedure and eligibility criteria_

The systematic review was planned, conducted, and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021). The identification and screening were done solely by the authors, no AI system or other screening algorithms were used. Our starting point was [Lintner’s (2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) systematic review, which provided a comprehensive evaluation of AI literacy instruments using the COSMIN framework. Lintner identified and assessed 16 AI literacy scales developed between 2021 and 2024, highlighting their structural properties, conceptual underpinnings, and limitations in areas such as content validity, cross-cultural applicability, and interpretability. His review offered a valuable synthesis of measurement quality but did not focus on syn- thesizing scale results or meta-analyzing empirical relationships be- tween AI literacy and related constructs.

PRISMA flowchart.

Building on this, we selected all 16 instruments identified by [Lintner (2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) as candidates for inclusion in our own synthesis. Following, we applied additional inclusion criteria focused on conceptual alignment with AI literacy as well as data availability. The instrument measuring “Intelligent TPACK” ([Çelik, 2023)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) was excluded for conceptual misalignment with the definition AI literacy. While this instrument in- corporates aspects of AI literacy, it primarily focuses on Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) specific to AI. The instrument assesses teachers’ integrated knowledge of how to effectively use AI tools to support pedagogical goals within specific subject areas. This includes not only understanding AI but also the pedagogical and content-related strategies for embedding AI tools into instruction. As such, it reflects a broader set of competencies than AI literacy alone. Consequently, the Intelligent TPACK instrument falls outside the scope of our review, which is focused specifically on instruments that target general-purpose AI literacy rather than pedagogical integration frame- works and competencies.

This resulted in a set of 15 core AI literacy instruments and their adaptions. To retrieve all publications that used one or more of these 15 instruments, we employed Google Scholar’s “Cited by” function. The search was conducted on February 3rd and 4th, 2025, resulting in an initial pool of 982 publications. After eliminating duplicates, 698 arti- cles remained. Next, we excluded non-English publications, leaving 576 articles. We then excluded all publications with “review” in the title, leaving 544 publications.

Subsequently, we attempted to access the abstract of every 

publication. Due to restricted access or missing abstracts, 15 publica- tions were excluded. Since the earliest publication of one of the in- struments is from 2022, all publications dating prior to 2022 (40 publications) were removed. The abstracts of the remaining 489 publi- cations were screened to determine whether it was an empirical study reporting original data. Publications not reporting empirical data (e.g., conceptual frameworks, opinion pieces, or policy documents) were excluded, resulting in the removal of 130 documents and leaving 359 studies that reported empirical research with original data. Next, we screened each publication to identify those reporting cor- relations with one of the AI literacy scales mentioned in the review. Some scales are multifactorial, such as the AILS scale by Wang et al. (2023), which comprises four factors (F1: awareness; F2: use; F3: eval- uation; and F4: ethics), while others are unidimensional (e.g., [Horn-](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) [berger et al., 2023](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) AI literacy test) or consist of three factors (e.g., [Laupichler et al. (2023;](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) ‘SNAIL’, Scale for the assessment of non-experts’ AI literacy). The instrument by [Carolus et al. (2023,](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) ‘MAILS’, Meta AI Literacy Scale) consists of four distinct _scales_, one of which measures AI literacy, while the others assess Ability to Create AI, AI Self-Efficacy, and AI Self-Management. For better comparability across studies, we excluded publications that reported correlations only with individual dimensions or subscales of AI literacy instruments rather than the full scale. This exclusion ensured that (1) all reported correlations capture the AI literacy construct in its entirety rather than a single facet (e.g., only technical terminology), and (2) the correlations are directly com- parable across instruments without being confounded by differences in dimensional coverage. In these excluded studies, only a subset of all items was used, often representing one dimension such as technical knowledge or ethical awareness, which limits the interpretability of the findings in relation to comprehensive AI literacy.

In summary, to be included, studies had to: (a) employ one of the 15 AI-literacy instruments (excluding “Intelligent TPACK”) identified in Lintner’s review or a validated adaptation; (b) report quantitative cor- relations between an overall AI-literacy score (not just a subscale) and at least one affective, behavioral, cognitive, or contextual variable; (c) report original empirical data (i.e., not conceptual papers or reviews); 

1. be written in English and accessible; and (e) be published 2022 or later as the earliest publication of one of the instruments is from 2022. Screening the full articles ultimately yielded 29 publications with 31 studies, as one publication ([Koch et al., 2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) reported three distinct studies on separate samples. The process following PRISMA is visualized in [Fig. 1.](#3-method)

### _3.2._ _Organizing variables by category_

For a more systematic analysis, we categorized all variables for

which correlations with AI literacy were reported using systematic content analysis. Variables representing similar constructs were grouped into categories, thereby structuring the extensive list of variables. As a general framework, we utilized the ABC (affective, behavioral, and cognitive variables) framework, extending it with an additional category labeled “Background and surrounding variables.” No data were lost during this merging process. The categorization was performed to facilitate the discussion of results. We acknowledge that alternative grouping frameworks, such as prominent models like TAM or the Uni- fied Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT, Venkatesh et al., 2003), could also be applicable. However, given the broad variety among the identified variables, we chose a broader, more inclusive approach.

### _3.3._ _Comparison of self-assessement and performance-based AI literacy scales_

To explore whether the type of AI literacy instrument (self-assesse- ment or performance-based) might influence the strength of reported correlations, we conducted a targeted comparison between self- assessment AI literacy scales and the performance-based multiple- choice AI literacy tests. We identified outcome variables for which bivariate correlations were reported using both instrument types across different studies. For each of these overlapping variables, we calculated a weighted average Pearson correlation coefficient using Fisher’s z- transformation ([Borenstein et al., 2021)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). This procedure accounts for differences in sample size across studies. The reported _r_ correlation values were transformed into z-scores, weighted by their corresponding study sample sizes, averaged, and then back-transformed to an _r_ esti- mate. The comparison includes three variables: positive AI attitudes, negative AI attitudes, and AI self-efficacy.

## 4. Results

### _4.1._ _Descriptive overview: Scope and characteristics of the reviewed studies (RQ1)_

The 31 studies in this review employed six different AI literacy in- struments or adaptions thereof. Eleven used Wang’s (2022) AI literacy instrument or its adaptations (AILS), seven used the MAILS AI literacy scale ([Carolus et al., 2023)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational), six used MAIRS or derivations ([Karaca et al., 2021)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational), three used Wang’s 2024 AI self-efficacy scale (AISE), two used the AI literacy instrument published by [Hornberger et al. (2023),](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) and two used the SNAILS instrument from [Laupichler et al. (2023).](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) In total, we identified 88 distinct scales for which the original studies reported correlations with one of these six AI literacy instruments.

the study involving IT leaders did not report a significant correlation, suggesting that the link between AI literacy and AI acceptance may vary 

across different populations or contexts.

**AI Attitudes**. The reviewed studies reveal a consistent trend where increased AI literacy is associated with more favorable attitudes toward AI ([Table 3)](#42-correlations-between-ai-literacy-and-affective-behavioral-cognitive-laupichler-et-al-2023-used-kendalls-τ-when-kendalls-τ-is-reported-and-contextual-variables-rq2-rq3--rq5-it-is-marked-in-the-following-tables-the-reviewed-studies-report-corre-). Studies employing the GAAIS (General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale) to measure AI attitudes indicate strong positive correlations between AI literacy and positive AI attitudes (ranging from 0.47 to 0.82) alongside corresponding negative correla- tions with negative AI attitudes (up to − 0.58), though the magnitude varies ([Fig. 2)](#422-behavioral-variables). Alternative measures of AI attitudes, such as those from the ATAISS and ATAI subscales, generally confirm that higher AI literacy is linked to more positive perceptions and lower levels of fear regarding AI. Moreover, the AILS instrument tends to yield higher correlations while studies involving other instruments, especially the AI literacy multiple-choice test by [Hornberger et al. (2023)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) show only modest 

correlations.

**Trust & Bias.** The reviewed studies indicate that higher AI literacy is generally associated with increased trust in AI, with significant positive correlations ranging from 0.29 to 0.539 observed among university teachers, college students, and other individuals ([Table 4)](#422-behavioral-variables). While [Kox and Beretta (2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) report that general trust is positively correlated with AI literacy, other trust and bias-related measures show no significant correlations with AI literacy. Among IT leaders, [Judkins et al. (2024)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) found a slight, non-significant negative correlation (− 0.13) between AI 

literacy and perceived trust.

**Motivation in AI-Supported Learning.** The studies consistently show robust, significant positive correlations between AI literacy and variables covering motivation in AI-supported learning ([Table 6)](#not-show-any-significant-correlation-with-ai-use-suggesting-potential-mindset-the-studies-reveal-that-ai-literacy-instruments-are-posi--differences-in-how-various-instruments-assess-ai-literacy-andor-ai-use-tively-correlated-with-mindset-related-constructs-exhibiting-moderate). Cor- relation values range from 0.350 up to 0.71. Highest correlations are observed among teachers (0.71), and moderate correlations are found among various student groups (ranging from 0.464 to 0.50 and 0.481).

hand-in-hand with its adoption. While the direction of influence, based on the correlations, remains unclear, the correlation implies that ini- tiatives raising literacy and opportunities for hands-on use could be mutually reinforcing. Correlations with participants’ age are weak and mostly non-significant, aligning with multiple findings from digital lit- eracy (Peng & Yu, 2022). This suggests that AI literacy, mostly measured within university student samples, may not be strongly shaped by age-related factors, than by educational interventions on cognitive, af- fective, and contextual factors. While our results showed no significant correlation between AI literacy and age, this may be due to the relatively narrow and student-dominated age ranges in the included studies (mean ages ranged from 21.4 to 33.3 years). Because the evidence base largely comes from higher-education contexts, age-related effects may still emerge in more diverse populations. Future studies should therefore test age - AI literacy correlations beyond the university setting.

### _5.3._ _Conflicting findings emerging from the reported studies on AI literacy correlations (RQ3)_

[Bewersdorff et al. (2025)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) report a non-significant correlation (0.00) between AI literacy and AI use, which challenges the notion of a “digital native” advantage. In contrast, other studies have found significant positive correlations between AI literacy and AI usage. This discrepancy may be attributable to differences in how “use” is defined and measured, as well as the type of AI literacy assessment employed - self-assessment versus performance-based measures.

Evidence regarding correlations of AI literacy with (perceived) trust and bias remains inconclusive. While some studies report a positive relationship between AI literacy and trust in AI, others find non- significant or even negative correlations. Higher AI literacy might not always lead to higher trust. Students with greater AI literacy might even distrust AI, despite acknowledging its usefulness (Pan et al., 2025). Trust in AI, as a construct, might be influenced by other factors, which com- plicates the interpretation of these correlations. The mixed results for trust and for “use” caution against digital-native assumptions: instruc- tional design should include trust-calibration and critical-use tasks, and institutions should avoid equating usage with literacy in targets or accountability. When evaluating programs and conducting studies re- searchers should report how “use” is defined, ideally agreeing on a standardized metric. Overall, these conflicting findings underscore the need for further research.

### _5.4._ _Influence of self-assessment vs. performance-based regarding the observed correlations (RQ4)_

The review reveals a notable difference in the observed correlations based on the measurement approach (see section [4.3)](#424-background-and-surrounding-variables-after-applying-z-transformation-and-weighting-the-correlation-pat-). Self-assessment scales might be vulnerable to metacognitive biases (e.g. when low per- formers overestimate their abilities) ([Brown, 1986;](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) [Dunning & Kruger, 1999)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational). These biases of self-assessment scales may lead to stronger cor- relations with affective variables (e.g., more positive attitudes), behav- ioral intentions (e.g., higher AI use), and cognitive constructs like AI 

Intention to use text-based Continuance ChatGPT-Continuance GenAI for learning intention intention

0.21 † ​ ​

​ ​ 0.54 †

​ ​ ​

​ 0.31\*\* ​

self-efficacy. As shown in section [4.3,](#424-background-and-surrounding-variables-after-applying-z-transformation-and-weighting-the-correlation-pat-) the correlation between AI self-efficacy and AI literacy is substantially higher when using self-assessment instruments (_r_ = _._84) compared to the performance-based multiple-choice test (_r_ = _._26). A similar, though slightly smaller, discrepancy emerges for positive AI attitudes, where self-assessment instruments yield _r_ = _._53 versus _r_ = _._20 for the performance-based measure. The performance-based test ([Hornberger et al., 2023)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) shows lower correlations with these self-reported variables. This suggests that self-assessment AI literacy scales may partly reflect AI self-efficacy or AI self-confidence rather than objective AI literacy. The MAILS AI literacy self-assessment scale ([Carolus et al., 2023)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) shows strong correlations with other self-assessment AI literacy scales (0.86; Pinski & Benlian, 2024 scale), but only weak correlations when compared with instruments like the AI literacy test by [Hornberger et al. (2023).](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) This further suggests that the measurement approach might influence the observed relationships. Self-assessment scales may have a tendency to capture self-perceived competence and self-efficacy, whereas performance-based tests tend to measure knowledge more objectively.

One variable for which the performance-based instrument yielded a weaker correlation than the self-assessment instruments was positive AI attitude. This inversion may reflect a social desirability bias in self- report ([Crowne & Marlowe, 1960)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) for information and communication technology (ICT) self-assessment (Palczynska ´ & Rynko, 2021): in- dividuals who rate themselves as highly AI literate may overreport their abilities and be reluctant to endorse negative or critical statements about AI, thereby dampening observed correlations with negatively framed items. Another explanation for the discrepancies could lie in the un- derlying construct coverage of the instruments. The AI literacy test by [Hornberger et al. (2023)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) is based on the [Long and Magerko (2020)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) set of competencies and measures slightly different AI literacy constructs (e.g., MAILS and AILS).

These findings highlight the need to investigate whether self- assessment and performance-based scales capture the same underlying construct of AI literacy and to clarify their assessment implications. This need is further underscored by the fact that the performance-based test has appeared in only two studies so far, albeit with sizable samples (each _N \>_ 1,000).

Because of the observed tendency that self-assessments inflate cor- relations with self-reported outcomes, it seems advisable that high- stakes decisions like curriculum evaluation, funding, and account- ability should not rely on self-assessment alone. The use performance- based tests or triangulation of different forms of assessment seems reasonable.

### _5.5._ _Research gaps regarding AI literacy scores and investigated variables (RQ5)_

Beyond the gaps mentioned in sections [5.1 to 5.4,](#51-scope-and-nature-of-the-studies-on-correlations-between-ai-literacy) additional research gaps exist. First, evidence linking AI literacy with gender is sparse, with only one study providing correlations between gender and AI literacy scores. Second, socio-economic factors have not been assessed in many 

studies. Although theories such as Bourdieu’s cultural capital suggest that socio-economic background could shape access to and proficiency in AI literacy, findings show little or no correlation of AI literacy with demographic factors. This low correlation might be partly a conse-

Use for Academic Support​ 0.234\*​ ​ ​ ​ ​ quence of the field’s reliance on relatively privileged university-student 

samples, where demographic variability is limited. Within these ho- mogeneous cohorts variation appears to arise instead from affective, 

& cognitive, and contextual factors. Third, surrounding factors such as 

institutional support structures and social influences are underexplored, despite indications that they play a critical role in the development and application of AI literacy ([Al-Amri & Al-Abdullatif, 2024;](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) Shen & Cui, 2024). Finally, little attention has been paid to the relationship between 

Use for displacement of traditional learing research​ 0.105\*​ ​ ​ ​ ​ interest in AI and AI literacy; in some studies it might be subsumed 

under broader motivation scales. Incorporating frameworks like the interest development model by [Hidi and Renninger (2006)](#study-are-available-from-the-corresponding-author-upon-reasonable-çayak-s-2024-investigating-the-relationship-between-teachers-attitudes-toward-request-artificial-intelligence-and-their-artificial-intelligence-literacy-journal-of-educational) could offer

## 6. Conclusion

Use of AI ​ ​ ​ 0.00 ​ ​ ​ This systematic review identified several variables that different AI 

literacy scales do and do _not_ correlate with. Our findings reveal many robust and strong correlations of AI literacy with variables such as AI self-efficacy and positive AI attitudes. This suggests that programs 

Prior use of AI ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ 0.49\*\*\* designed to boost AI literacy should deliberately target both 

competence-building and attitude-shaping components to maximize their impact. Age and most other demographic factors show little or no correlation with AI literacy in the predominantly university-student 

Use in everyday life ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ 0.34\*\*\*​ samples reviewed. For this rather privileged population, efforts to 

strengthen AI literacy should target affective, behavioral, and cognitive and contextual factors rather than demographic characteristics. For re- searchers, the robust correlations of AI literacy with affective, behav- ioral, cognitive, and contextual factors, contrasted with the weak 

Use at school/ university​ ​ ​ ​ ​ 0.29\*\*\*​ correlations for demographic characteristics, could encourage a more 

nuanced investigation into AI literacy through broader and more diverse sample populations. This could help to deepen our understanding of AI literacy as it evolves over time and in diverse groups aside from uni-

Use at work ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ 0.35\*\*\*​

versity students, thereby providing more comprehensive insights that 

reflect differences across professional and cultural backgrounds.

The review uncovered some measurement challenges regarding AI literacy. Correlations derived from self-assessment scales are systemat- ically stronger than those obtained with a performance-based multiple- choice test. This pattern is particularly evident for AI self-efficacy and 

Use frequency (to learn 2nd language)​ ​ 0.281\*\*​ ​ ​ ​

positive AI attitudes. This suggests that differences in measurement approaches can influence the observed strengths of correlations. Self- 

N 1465 assessment scales, while efficient, may be influenced by metacognitive 

biases, potentially inflating correlations with self-reported outcomes. Addressing these methodological issues (e.g. by triangulation of self- ratings with objective tests) will be critical for ensuring that future 

no p-value provided.research accurately captures AI literacy. Target groupuniversity studentscollege studentscollege studentsuniversity studentspersonsindividualsindividuals† Despite these psychometric challenges, educators can build on our 

findings by pairing AI literacy instruction with affective and behavioral .001, _\<_ components, helping learners engage with AI in informed, reflective, _p_ and self-determined ways. Expanding courses and research beyond
